questions.q: What are the three parts every Sentinel Automation Rule has?
options: Workspace, region, and resource group
Entity, analytic rule, and watchlist
Trigger, conditions, and actions
Connector, parameter, and schema
questions.explain: An Automation Rule always has a trigger (e.g. incident created), a set of AND/OR conditions evaluated against the incident, and actions such as running a playbook.

questions.q: What does the Microsoft Sentinel connector's "Microsoft Sentinel incident" trigger hand to a Logic App playbook?
options: The full incident object, including its ARM ID, severity, title, and extracted entities
Nothing -- the playbook must call Get_incident first before any data is available
Only the incident's severity level as a plain string
A pre-filled containment action that must be approved or rejected
questions.explain: The trigger hands the workflow the full incident object the moment Sentinel calls it, including the ARM ID, severity, title, and entity list.

questions.q: In the Logic App workflow definition shown in this lesson, what does `runAfter` control?
options: Which Azure region the Logic App deploys into
The condition logic inside the Sentinel Automation Rule itself
The role-based access control assignment on the Logic App's resource group
How sequencing between actions works -- an action runs only once the actions it depends on have succeeded
questions.explain: runAfter expresses the dependency and sequencing between workflow actions, so Add_comment_to_incident only fires after Get_incident succeeds.

questions.q: Why might Sentinel prompt you to grant a role on the Logic App's resource group the first time you add it as an Automation Rule action?
options: Because Logic Apps require a paid HSM-backed key vault before they can run
Because Sentinel needs explicit permission to invoke that specific playbook, and without it the trigger call is rejected
Because the playbook will otherwise auto-delete itself after one run
Because incident comments cannot be written without a global administrator role
questions.explain: Sentinel needs the Microsoft Sentinel Automation Contributor role on the playbook's resource group; without it, the Automation Rule's call to run the playbook is rejected.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the most reliable way to debug a Sentinel playbook that didn't seem to do anything?
options: Check the Logic Apps Run history blade, where each action shows its raw inputs and outputs
Guess which action failed and rewrite the whole playbook from scratch
Wait for another real incident and see if it behaves differently
Delete the Automation Rule and recreate it with the same settings
questions.explain: Run history shows each action's status, inputs, and outputs, so a failed step like Get_incident is visible immediately instead of producing a vague symptom.
